items.text: SEASON 8 · EPISODE 5 · DRAFT · CASE-044  The main equipment room · Maya, Kit, Bram and Aurelio (the mechanical engineer) · Level L5 · Advanced support (formulas on request)  The main equipment room is at 38 °C with burn-in only half loaded. Its cooling was designed for a sixth of what’s in it.  ⚑ RV-160: cooling is the mechanical engineer’s; fire doors stay shut. RV-161: figures illustrative. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Heat
items.stakes: The main equipment room is at 38 °C with burn-in half loaded. The cooling was designed for a sixth of the load.
items.clock: Before full burn-in in ten days.
items.reward: A room that holds its temperature with one cooling unit out — and a number that never goes unsent again.

objectives.text: Find where the cooling went wrong

items.alt: The main equipment room: heat shimmer over the racks, a wall thermometer reading 38 °C; Kit points at it; Maya in the doorway.

bubbles.text: Then the room was designed for something else.

items.caption: Full burn-in in ten days.

lines.text: Then the room was designed for something else. Let's find out what.

items.prompt: 14:15. The racks are throttling. What happens right now?
unknown: What the cooling was sized for
items.risk: Damaged equipment — or an untested building on preview night.
timeout: Someone props the door with a fire extinguisher.
Bram's safety walk finds it at four.

hints.text: What protects the gear now — and whose is the cooling?

options.label: Prop the MER door open and bring in fans
options.result: Bram: “That's a fire door. It stays shut.”
options.consequence: Breaks a fire separation to cool a room.

options.label: Put a logger in the room alarming to operations; ask the AV contractor to cut burn-in to what the room can carry; ask the GC to get the mechanical engineer on it today
options.result: Burn-in at 30%; the logger shows the trend; Aurelio calls back within the hour.
options.consequence: Protect the equipment, measure, and bring in the owner of cooling.

options.label: Keep burn-in running — throttling is what protects them
options.result: Two power supplies fail by Wednesday.

options.label: Switch everything off until opening
options.result: No burn-in; the first real load is the preview.
options.consequence: Safe today, blind on the night.

items.title: The number nobody sent.
items.body: Aurelio, the mechanical engineer, sized the MER for 2 kW — from equipment list 03, two years old: two racks and no broadcast room. The racks now draw 12.8 kW, about 43,700 BTU an hour. The design team's AV heat schedule sits in its transmittal log marked ‘draft — not issued’. The gap between two disciplines was on Maya's side.
items.label: Test: how far over — and whose gap?

items.sub: Advanced · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Kit beside a board. Twelve point eight kilowatts of racks. The mechanical design assumed two. What's that in the units the mechanical engineer uses? Times three point four one two — about forty-three thousand seven hundred BTU an hour. And with two seven-kilowatt units, if one fails, seven isn't enough. So three: N plus one. She sizes it. We owe her the heat schedule we never sent.

items.caption: Advanced: the formula is there if you ask. Try without it first.

items.text: 📙 ON REQUEST · ADVANCED  Terms   Heat load   N+1   Basis of design   If you need it   ƒ Ask for the formula · Equipment heat load   ƒ FORMULA · Equipment heat load  Q BTU/h  = P W  × 3.412   P W   electrical power the equipment draws, W  Q BTU/h   heat released into the room, BTU per hour  3.412  BTU/h per watt      ƒ Ask for the formula · N+1 cooling   ƒ FORMULA · N+1 cooling  C × (N − 1) ≥ Q   C  capacity of one cooling unit, kW  N  number of units  Q  heat load, kW

items.label: **Learn it now:** heat loads, cooling and N+1.

items.label: **Find it:** where did the MER lose its cooling?

items.title: N+1.
items.body: With the heat schedule in hand, Aurelio proposes two 7 kW units: 14 kW against 12.8. On a normal night, fine. But units get serviced, and they fail. With one out, 7 kW faces 12.8 kW of racks — on the preview night, the broadcast room goes first.
items.label: Test: what's left with one unit out — and who selects the units?
**Work it out:** cool the MER so one unit can fail.

items.prompt: Tuesday. What do you ask Aurelio for?
unknown: Lead time for a third unit
items.risk: A preview night one fan belt away from failure.
timeout: The order for two units goes in.
The redundancy question comes back after opening.

hints.text: What does the room need when one unit is out?

options.label: Accept two 7 kW units — 14 kW covers 12.8
options.result: The first maintenance visit takes the MER to 35 °C.

options.label: N+1: enough units that one can be out and the rest carry 12.8 kW — three of her 7 kW units — her sizing and selection, with your diversity and growth figures; temporary spot cooling from the mechanical sub until they arrive
options.result: Aurelio re-selects three; the GC sequences them for next week; spot cooling arrives Wednesday.
options.consequence: One can fail; the room still holds.

options.label: One 15 kW unit
options.result: One unit, one failure, one dark night.

options.label: Move the racks to the stage basement
options.result: Odile: “That's a trap room, not an equipment room.”
options.consequence: Moves the problem, breaks the building.

items.title: Weather made to order
items.body: In 1902 a young engineer designed a system to control the humidity in a printing plant in Brooklyn, so paper wouldn't swell between one colour and the next. It is usually counted as the first modern air conditioning. It was sized from a number — how much moisture and heat the room had to lose. Every cooling design since starts the same way.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #76 · AVERY'S LENS  Hand over the numbers others size from  If another discipline sizes its design from your numbers, sending them — and confirming they arrived — is part of your design.  The mechanical engineer cooled the MER for 2 kW because nobody sent her the 12.8 kW heat schedule. Her design was right for what she was told.

items.alt: A cooling sheet after the fix: heat load 12.8 kW; three 7 kW units give 21 kW; with one unit out, 14 kW, past the load line; heat schedule issued and acknowledged; full load with one unit off: 26 °C.
items.caption: One unit out, and the room holds.

items.prompt: Friday. How do numbers cross between disciplines from now on?
timeout: The broadcast room's power schedule stays in draft.

hints.text: What else does another engineer size from your work?

options.label: Every number another discipline sizes from — heat, power, weight, data — goes on a coordination register; each is issued, and the receiving engineer acknowledges it
options.result: Aurelio adds her side's list; Varga adds power; Kit owns the register.
options.consequence: Send it, and confirm it landed.

options.label: Mechanical should ask us next time
options.result: They didn't know there was anything to ask about.
options.consequence: Puts the gap on the side that couldn't see it.

options.label: Nothing — it's fixed
options.result: The broadcast room's power schedule is next.

Forty-one numbers somebody else is building from.

items.prompt: The heat schedule was ours, wasn't it. Our side never sent it.

options.label: “Ours. So we send it today, with the numbers, and we ask Aurelio to confirm she has it. Then we fix how numbers cross over.”
options.reply: Sending it now. With a read receipt and a phone call.

options.label: “It was before our time.”
options.reply: The job isn't before our time.

options.label: “Mechanical should have asked.”
options.reply: Maybe. They're not the ones who knew.

items.title: MER: 2 kW
items.body: The mechanical basis of design, rev 1, two years ago: ‘MER — AV/IT equipment 2 kW (per equipment list 03).’ Equipment list 03 had two racks and no broadcast room.

items.alt: The lobby: a video wall of displays, every other one black; Kit points; Maya stares.

bubbles.text: Half the lobby screens are black. Two shipments, two firmwares.

items.title: heat schedule · draft
items.body: The design team's transmittal log: ‘AV heat schedule — DRAFT — not issued’. Last edited by the previous design lead the week she left.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Every watt a rack draws becomes heat: Q = P × 3.412 BTU/h. Cooling is sized by the mechanical engineer from your heat schedule — so issue it, and confirm it arrived. N+1: C × (N − 1) ≥ Q, so the room survives one unit out. Fire doors stay shut. Put every number another discipline sizes from on a register the receiving engineer acknowledges.
REFLECTION (optional)  · What number do you own that somebody else is quietly building on?
